items.en: Meta recently updated its commercial terms of use, declaring that the company can “use any content from [a business account’s] domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of” Meta products and services.

According to legal experts interviewed by Nieman Lab, this looked like a “remarkable provision” that could give Meta permission to scrape the website of any publisher with a Meta business account and use the content to train the company’s AI models. (While Meta defeated a high-profile lawsuit over alleged copyright infringement last year, other cases against AI companies, including Meta, continue.)
However, a Meta spokesperson insisted that the updated terms did not reflect a change in the way Meta crawls the web. And now, The Verge reports that the provision has been removed.

“We’ve heard you and want to clarify: the crawling terms we consolidated only applied to our ads and business products, and we’ve clarified that in the terms themselves,” the company said in a statement. “It does not change how Meta uses web crawlers.”

More than 5 million people around the world have an advanced form of age-related macular degeneration (AMD) called geographic atrophy, in which cells in the retinas die off. And until now, no treatment could restore their vision. The PRIMA system, which was approved in Europe in July and is awaiting FDA clearance in the US, changes that. It combines a retinal implant with camera-equipped eyeglasses to improve sight in patients who develop a blind spot in the middle of their vision due to advanced AMD. After training sessions, more than 80% of recipients were able to read, do crosswords, and use their phones.

Developed by the California-based Science Corporation, the system takes advantage of the fact that AMD doesn’t damage all retinal circuitry; only photoreceptors—the cells that convert light into an electrical signal—die off. PRIMA’s implant mimics those cells and transmits visual information directly to healthy eye circuitry and on to the brain. “We’re leveraging all of the body’s own natural functions to process and transmit the information,” says Frank Brodie, an ophthalmologist at the University of California, San Francisco, and Science Corp.'s chief medical officer for ophthalmology.

Glasses outfitted with a miniature front-facing camera capture what someone is seeing in real time. The video feed is roughly five megapixels running at 30 frames per second, which is similar to TV. The raw video is transmitted to a connected processor via a fiber-optic cable.

A small, handheld processor, which can be set on a table or tucked in a pocket, converts the video feed into infrared light signals that route back to the glasses. The device also includes physical buttons that let the wearer adjust contrast, brightness, and zoom.

A laser projector on the glasses faces the wearer and shines pulses of near-infrared light directly at the eye at 880 nanometers—an invisible wavelength. This signal passes through the pupil and on to the retinal implant in the back of the eye.

The implant is made up of 378 pixels, each with an electrode and two photovoltaic cells, which do double duty. They convert the light into a current that healthy bipolar and ganglion cells pass on to the brain. They also act as solar cells to power the chip, eliminating the need for a battery.
Update: This story has been updated to clarify the specific cases of AMD the PRIMA system treats.
Linda Marsa is a former Los Angeles Times reporter and an author who covers medicine, health, science, and the environment.

The Elizabeth Holmes of You Can See Everything is not the turtlenecked tech visionary from the Forbes cover, the awkward dancer depicted in the The Dropout, or the criminal defendant showing up to federal court in princess curls. The Elizabeth Holmes you see in A24’s mind-warping new documentary is a different woman. She’s a devoted mom and wife. She wears calm, neutral colors. Call her Liz.

She’s also 35 days away from incarceration. In 2022, the disgraced former Theranos CEO was sentenced to 11 years in prison for defrauding investors; seven years earlier, federal regulators and The Wall Street Journal had delivered the bombshell revelation that Theranos’s revolutionary blood-testing technology that purported to run hundreds of lab tests on a single blood prick did not, in fact, work. Holmes stayed silent, convinced of her innocence. But eventually, Holmes and her husband, Billy Evans, approached A24 for a documentary, believing that radical exposure would clear her name. Miraculously and unbelievably, the couple opened their San Diego home to Nathan Fielder — not a journalist but a cringe comedian now invited to live alongside one of the most cringe subjects of all. Manipulator, meet manipulator. Alongside his co-director, Lance Oppenheim, and their film crew, they accomplished the impossible: illuminating something new about Holmes, when both metaphorically and literally, her case seemed to be closed.

You Can See Everything makes Holmes appear strangely sympathetic — even as Fielder repeatedly interrogates this sympathy. If the Holmes of the early 2010s was obsessed with Silicon Valley masculinity, here she is a paragon of white femininity — fragile, innocent, incapable of harm. Holmes carries herself with an unsettling guilelessness, her uncanny blue eyes wide and unblinking. Under certain lighting, her blonde hair resembles a halo. We see scenes of Holmes swimming in the ocean, reading to her small children, and panicking over her imminent separation from her family. Throughout, she insists on her pure intentions. She wants to start a new Theranos, she says, to save millions of lives.

At times, she speaks with the dazed acceptance of a trauma survivor with amnesia, the victim of an unnamed tragedy, the depths of which she has yet to confront. She tears up suddenly. Her most frequent reply to Fielder’s questions is: “I don’t know.” In one scene, Fielder asks her father, Christian — a former Enron executive — what went wrong. He references the alleged rape that caused Holmes to drop out of Stanford, only to never return to the subject in the documentary again.

Holmes’s husband acts as both guardian and publicist; in one notable scene, he yanks a bowl of raw eggs out of her hands, because he thinks she’s whisking it too slowly. In another, Evans praises her as “special” after she appears incapable of processing Abbott and Costello’s classic comedy routine “Who’s on First?” It’s the type of cooing, offensive euphemism sometimes used to describe people with disabilities. It’s also in this scene that Holmes reduces her deception to an error of interpretation. When she said that Theranos could run hundreds of lab tests, she didn’t mean it was capable at that moment; she meant that it was in the realm of possibility — it could be in the future. But did Holmes know that this was technically false, or was she not capable of understanding the difference between what she said and how it was perceived?

This narrative aligns with the portrait she and her lawyers sketched in her criminal defense trial, where they offloaded blame onto Theranos’s co-founder Ramesh “Sunny” Balwani, Holmes’s much-older partner of 12 years. In unsealed court filings, her defense team accused him of “dominating her and erasing her capacity to make decisions,” a subject of intimate partner abuse, depression, and post-traumatic stress disorder. “He wasn’t who I thought he was,” Holmes testified on the stand. In You Can See Everything, Evans replaces Balwani as puppeteer — and it’s really in the latter half of the three-hour film, when it zooms in on Evans, that you start to question Holmes’s culpability. We learn that Evans attempted to negotiate payment from A24 for the documentary, seemingly without his wife’s knowledge, even though she tells Fielder on-camera she’s not motivated by money. Once Holmes is in prison, Evans tweets under her name on her X account and creates an AI deepfake of her — a clear violation of consent. In another meta twist, Fielder dramatizes his visit to Holmes in federal prison where he tries to warn her, but he believes she seems unperturbed by it. The woman he sees, smiling at her husband and kids, is one blinded by love.
The documentary provides more questions than answers: Sure, you can see everything — but can you trust what you see?

A previous version of this post incorrectly stated that Billy Evans had successfully negotiated payment from A24 and that it happened without Elizabeth Holmes’s knowledge. We have amended it to reflect that it was only an attempted negotiation, and that its unclear whether Holmes was indeed not aware.

Among the many cinematic influences swirling around in Lance Oppenheim and Nathan Fielder’s Elizabeth Holmes documentary You Can See Everything, one emerges about halfway through the movie when a new blonde woman enters the narrative. Oh my God, they’re doing Vertigo, I thought to myself while watching. In the 1958 Hitchcock film, the apparent death of one woman played by Kim Novak leads Jimmy Stewart to find a new woman and mold her into the one he lost. Holmes, the former founder of Theranos who was found guilty on four counts of fraud in 2022 and who insists on her innocence throughout the documentary, begins her 11-year sentence in a federal prison in Texas. Since Oppenheim and Fielder can’t record her there, their contact is mediated through her seemingly unstable and controlling husband, Billy Evans. In an attempt to uncover what might be going on in her mind, Fielder travels to a farm in upstate New York to meet actress Amanda Seyfried, who played Holmes to much acclaim in the 2022 Hulu series The Dropout. Can someone who understands how to perform an idea of Holmes help Fielder and Oppenheim understand her as a person?

Seyfried turns out to be an essential aspect of You Can See Everything’s success as a film. She provides an invaluable counterbalance to Fielder and Oppenheim’s approach as both a commentator on Holmes’s persona and someone who, as a different kind of artist than Fielder and Oppenheim, has an orthogonal approach to thinking about the truth. Prior to her arrival, the film is confined largely to the claustrophobic rented California beach bungalow where Fielder and the documentary team spend time with Holmes, her husband, and their children. When Fielder plays some of that footage back for Seyfried on-camera — including a lasagna of a sequence where Seyfried watches Holmes watch The Dropout — she, a much more freely emotive person than Fielder, reacts out loud by saying many of the things that the audience might have been thinking earlier. It is weird how Holmes and Evans behave, Evans does come off as sinister, and it is funny how Holmes doesn’t seem to know how to beat eggs.

But Seyfried also contributes her expertise as an actor. At the end of the scene where she reviews that footage with Fielder, she starts to imitate Holmes’s lower voice and bearing, repeating some of her performance in The Dropout. Soon, in a sequence that recalls Fielder’s experiments with reenactments on The Rehearsal, he returns to that bungalow with Seyfried to re-create scenes from his time with Holmes — and in a scene that definitely recalls Vertigo, you see Seyfried getting her hair and makeup done to become Holmes. The idea is that, as an actor, she might be able to work backward to her subject’s psychology — you may also note the added tension of Holmes contesting a quote attributed to her in an article in which she says she was playing a character herself during her time at Theranos. Seyfried, now literally playing a character in playing Holmes, also fills in for moments that Oppenheim didn’t or couldn’t record. In a later sequence, with the help of Christopher Abbott, who plays Evans less aptly than Seyfried can nail Holmes, she re-creates the tense negotiation between Fielder, Oppenheim, Evans, Holmes, and executives from the movie’s studio A24. There, Seyfried plays out Fielder’s memory of Holmes leaving the room before Evans demands to be paid to participate in the documentary. (The producers agree to it, but the film later reveals that Evans ceded his stake after Fielder encouraged him to do so.) The reenactment probes a knotty question at the heart of the doc: Is Holmes as innocent as she says she is? And whether her claims of trustworthiness are a posture or not, does she knowingly let men like Evans do dirty work for her? It’s not something the film can definitely answer, but Seyfried’s performance allows the doc to sketch out some plausible answers. It’s a deft, haunting, complicated bit of work, which gets more detailed as she and Fielder discuss what they’ve learned about Holmes from his time with her. As on television, Seyfried nails Holmes’s wide eyes, unsteady mannerisms, deep voice, and mysterious vocal cadence that makes the character both unreal and oddly human. A friend of mine watching the film next to me wondered aloud if she might win an Oscar for it. (Would A24 have to campaign her only for the acting portion of the documentary? Is it possible to make a case for that?)

That would be fun, but the particular muddiness of You Can See Everything makes Seyfried as much a subject as a participant. She doesn’t just agree to play scenes as Holmes; she also joins Fielder on a trip to Texas to meet with Evans and probe him for answers about his relationship with his incarcerated partner. In that scene, Fielder, Evans, and Seyfried share dinner and drinks at Evans’s house, and Evans ambushes them — and, seemingly, Holmes herself — by putting a call from the prison on speaker so that Holmes is suddenly speaking to the woman who played her in a television series that she insists deeply upset her. The cameras capture Seyfried sinking into a couch with embarrassment as she tries to come up with something to say to Holmes. (She compliments her family.) Unlike Fielder, who has faced Holmes directly, Seyfried has only gotten to know her in the abstract.

The rest of that encounter is charged with the discomfort of Evans’s open distrust of Seyfried and Seyfried’s own defensiveness of her work. At one point, Seyfried starts to sound a bit like Holmes in the way she equivocates around the fact that she didn’t exactly play Elizabeth Holmes on The Dropout, but played a character suggested by the podcast reporting and other available materials that the series relied on. (We never do hear from other members of the creative team on that show about how they might feel about Holmes’s response to it, or Seyfried’s decision to get in touch with Evans, another thorn among the complications of the movie.) Evans, at that dinner, sees Seyfried and Fielder as two kinds of vultures, though to him, she may be the more dangerous one. He can negotiate with Fielder about his work in process; she has already released something he can’t control at all. The fact that Seyfried is a woman seems to bring out a side of Evans he hasn’t shown to Fielder and Oppenheim. Toward Seyfried, he turns petty and spiteful, implying that she’s a coastal elite actor who preyed on his wife’s misfortune and saying that she has no sense of the actual spirit of the country because she publicly criticized Charlie Kirk after his death — though thanks to shifting politics and the fact that Kirk’s death has become memed into absurdity a year later, that line now plays to Seyfried’s favor. That’s also another beat in the documentary where Evans and Holmes seem to misread or misunderstand popular culture, humor, or art. Evans, bafflingly, had thought of Fielder as the man he wanted to do a documentary about him and his wife after watching Nathan for You, a show about business scams. Holmes, in a wild early sequence, doesn’t seem to understand the basic premise of Abbott and Costello’s “Who’s on first?” bit. It’s like seeing people who skipped all their liberal arts classes in school. They make pie-in-the-sky claims about their skill in science and technology but get antsy, vague, and pedantic about what their own words might mean or how they might come across as characters themselves. That’s probably what sets them off about Seyfried too; artists are dangerous people to be around, especially if you don’t know — or don’t want — to interpret yourself.

Seyfried’s involvement in the doc summits in its beguiling final sequence, which positions Fielder and Seyfried as two sides of a conversation about what kind of person Holmes is. Desperate for actual contact with Holmes, Fielder has arranged to meet her briefly at the prison before Evans shows up. Fielder can’t record that conversation, so he writes it down afterward to the best of his ability, returns to Seyfried’s farm to discuss it, then has her reenact it with him. That scene falls at the breaking point between documentary and narrative fiction and reminded me of what actress Merritt Wever, who appeared in Oppenheim’s fictional movie Primetime, told me about how she and Oppenheim debated their differing approaches to truth. As a documentarian, Oppenheim felt that truth is what can be captured through preparation and sometimes by accident on relatively objective devices — cameras, microphones. Wever, or an actor like Seyfried, argue through their work that you can arrive at another valuable, if subjective, emotional truth by channeling some sense of interiority as an artist.

When Fielder and Seyfried sit together in chairs by a fire at her farm and go over his last conversation with Holmes, what they’re doing is essentially a scene study. They scrutinize certain lines, talk about motivation, and wonder about how the scene might play with slight modifications. It’s also, compellingly, the moment they seem to trade sympathies. Seyfried came across as more sympathetic to Holmes earlier in the film, but now appears ruffled by her encounter with Evans and frustrated by Holmes’s dislike of The Dropout (as well as the fact that she mispronounces her last name), and she clocks that Fielder has, in spending so much time with Holmes, grown softer toward his subject. Seyfried notices that Fielder’s recollection is inexact, that he has allowed wiggle room for Holmes to maintain deniability about her knowledge of Evans’s actions through his written scene. The breakdown of communication between Oppenheim and Fielder and Holmes and Evans might make it impossible to get to the truth of Holmes. But the way in which You Can See Everything gives space to Seyfried’s perspective made me oddly, warmly hopeful. The documentary contains, through her participation and performance, the accommodation that facts alone are insufficient and maybe impossible. We also have to understand ourselves through art.

It was a sleepy, off-season Friday night in Bridgehampton in early October, but at the French bistro Almond, a rowdy crowd of East End gay guys were drinking, swaying to George Michael, and thirsting over Chris Gallant, the 37-year-old Democrat currently running to represent them in Congress. He arrived shortly before 9 p.m. wearing blue jeans and a plaid button-up that accentuated his biceps, ordered a dirty Hendrick’s martini, and quickly got to work, shaking hands, kissing cheeks, and posing for photographs with his would-be constituents. It was his eighth event of the day, but he didn’t seem tired, even as his presence turned the restaurant into a hot and bothered gay petting zoo. When he finally sat down, he almost immediately had to get up again. “Before I go, can I get a picture? For my website? I mean, my Instagram page?” a silver-haired gay in a Hawaiian shirt, apparently a local politician from Southampton, asked him. Soon after, the restaurant’s owner, who met Gallant on Fire Island, came over to show him a text he’d just received: “When is that sexy helicopter daddy going to be there?” Word about his presence had spread on social media. Gallant blushed and waved him away. “I never imagined I would be international news,” he told me, a little bashfully. “I hate some of those pictures of me. But the world thought it was hot as shit.”

It’s been a particularly dramatic few weeks for Gallant, a first-time candidate for public office. In mid-September, the New York Post ran a story about his “secret BDSM past,” revealing the existence of a number of “racy” images of him that had surfaced on the internet. It was a relatively PG way to characterize the photos, which had been taken in San Francisco in 2010. In some, Gallant can be seen posing in his tighty-whities and mugging for the camera in a “posture collar” and a leather harness; in others, he’s performing oral sex, receiving oral sex, and, somewhat impressively, seemingly performing oral sex on himself. Almost everyone at Almond seemed to have seen them — and definitely enjoyed them. “If he looked bad in the photos, this might be a different story,” one admirer at the bar told me. “Oh, he’s hot. Let’s vote for him.”

But horny gays aren’t the only voters in New York’s First Congressional District, a reliably Republican stretch of Long Island that hasn’t been represented by a Democrat in over a decade. Before the photos came out, Gallant had seemed a promising candidate — centrist and clean-cut enough to face off against the current representative, Nick LaLota, a Republican who handily beat the former CNN pundit John Avlon in 2024. When Gallant launched his campaign last August, he introduced himself to voters as a proud gun owner and former air-traffic controller, union leader, volunteer firefighter, and military man who joined the National Guard as a teenager after 9/11 and later flew a Black Hawk helicopter in Kuwait. “I literally signed a blank check that was up to and including my life for this country,” he told me at one point, as if he were out stumping on the trail. After Gallant won his primary in June, against a 25-year-old, pro-Palestine progressive, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee labeled the race as “in play.”

In his campaign ads, Gallant came across as your standard Long Island bro: They showed him driving motorcycles, grilling steaks, drinking beer, riding around in a fire truck, and posing in front of American flags. Though the biography on his campaign website included one sentence about a fiancé named Mike, he did not talk about his sexuality on the trail. “I didn’t hide from it, but I never said anything about it,” he told me. “I didn’t run because I’m gay. I’m running on the issues,” which he identified as “housing, groceries, gas prices, corrupt government, and politicians that don’t want to do their damn job.” Now, he’s having to reintroduce himself as not only the tough-looking Channing Tatum type with a crew cut and blandly Establishment Dem talking points — “Trump 1 was bad, but there were guardrails. Trump 2? There’s no guardrails!” — but the out gay guy who once voluntarily let himself be photographed inside of a cage while being penetrated from behind. “I remember like it was yesterday,” he told me at Almond, between sips of his martini, not showing any signs of embarrassment. “It was fun. It was great. I had a lot of fun.”

When the photos first leaked, Gallant says, “My heart stopped. I was like, Fuck. What do we do? Let’s take a breath. I need a fucking cocktail.” He called his campaign team, who he says encouraged him to drop out of the race — what most aspiring politicians would do if over a dozen professional photographs of them erect and naked leaked. Gallant disagreed. “I said, ‘Fuck it. Yeah, that’s me. I’m not going to deny it. I’m totally unashamed of it. It’s who I am,’” he told me, a sentiment he continued to repeat, over and over again, throughout our night together, especially after another drink or two. “I’m just me,” he said at one point, before repeating himself three more times.

Even as The Daily Show cracked jokes (“This guy is going to make a great House majority whip”) and the right worked itself into a frenzy (“Most Americans are Normal People and they are rightly creeped out by this stuff,” wrote a pundit in Breitbart), Gallant’s team put out merch that read “Make Politics Sexy Again” and sent him on TMZ. Gallant seemed comforted by the consensus of the gay internet — that he is hot and maybe even a little relatable. What gay guy with a Grindr hasn’t been photographed in a compromising position and, in some cases, widely disseminated those nudes himself? Still, he told me, he’d at least taken some measures to prevent this from happening in the first place. Before he decided to run, he says, “advisers” in the Democratic Party encouraged him to “scrub” his social media, starting with his profile picture on Instagram, which showed him in a pink Speedo in Mykonos. It’s not that he was embarrassed or ashamed of all that thirst trapping, he says; rather, he thought it would be best to make himself seem more “serious,” by which he probably meant “electable,” especially on Long Island. Apparently, he didn’t try that hard. “I very much so knew those photos existed,” he told me. “I mean, I have them all on my phone. It wasn’t something I hadn’t seen in a couple of months or something. We all have a lot of photos on our phone, especially in the gay world.”

Gallant has long had to straddle those two worlds, the gay and the straight. He first joined the National Guard at 17, and two years later he was working at Splash Bar, a gay nightclub in Chelsea, from Thursdays to Saturdays for Twink Night, Muscle Night, and BDSM Night. (He easily qualified for all three.) At the end of his shift on Saturday, he says he’d often head straight to Fire Island, where he bartended at Sip N Twirl over the summers. “We’d have a limo waiting out front of the club,” he told me. “I’d fill the limo with boys and booze and we’d be on the first ferry the next morning and we’d just have a fucking blast.” Still today, he brags, “I could probably go out in Hell’s Kitchen and not pay for a goddamn drink.” When we spoke, he told me he’d been back in the Pines just two weeks beforehand for a fundraiser — though, unlike most of the queens from the city, he drove his own boat instead of taking the ferry.

Gallant gives the impression that he wasn’t all that shy about his sexuality during both his deployments. When recounting his most recent time overseas, it often sounds like something from a military-themed porno — or Pete Hegseth’s worst nightmare. “Let me put it this way: I was one of the few that were actually getting laid regularly,” he told me. His call sign in the Army was “Notch,” which had a double meaning. For one, he put a lot of notches in his belt on the base (which is where he met his fiancé, who is still stationed overseas). There was even an acronym for it: “Never Once Touched Cunt Hair.” “These military men? They’re fucking horny. And there’s not many options,” he told me. “Gays get away with whatever the fuck they want, really, in the military.”

He’s never been shy about his sex life, but then again, he says he had no aspirations toward public office at the time. “I never imagined getting into politics, really,” he told me. “My mom used to tell me as a kid all the time, ‘I could see you being president,’ but that’s just a thing mothers say.” His mother was prescient about other things too. “She says she’s known I was gay since I was 10,” he says. He came out at 15. “I tell her all the time, ‘You’re the reason I’m a homo because you’re a pain in the ass.’”

He doesn’t believe his occasionally promiscuous past should be disqualifying. “As gay people, we’ve got rules, which are very different than the heteros, the heterosexual world of things,” he told me. “I just think we’re living in the New Age now.” One in which, he predicts, there will be plenty more situations like his. “There’s so many good people that want to run for office that are afraid of their naked pictures coming out. That’s a problem.” Just look at the current members of Congress, he said, who are “dying in their seats.” “They didn’t have the internet. They didn’t have pictures and all these things we have today, our generation,” he told me. “If I have to be the person to wear the banner and make this breakthrough, I’m going to do it.”

At the end of the night, Gallant got behind the bar to sling cocktails, shaking up dozens of perfectly blush-pink Cosmopolitans for his supporters. By then, he’d unbuttoned his shirt a couple notches and had moved on from martinis to white wine — not the brewskis in his ads. The gays at the bar snapped photo after photo of him; almost everyone I talked to was hesitant to call what he was going through a scandal. “Everybody age 38 and younger is like, Whatever, all our nudes are out on the internet, not a big deal, nobody cares,” one onlooker told me. “Honey, look at the other side. The Republicans? Half of them are pedophiles, thieves, war criminals, animal murderers, or dog murderers. They’re a thousand times more scandalous.” Michael Koegler, the chair of the East Hampton Democratic Committee, who was at the bar ordering a Shirley Temple, agreed. “Fifteen years ago, it might’ve been this huge scandal. Chris is who he is. He’s not afraid of his sexuality. You know what? No one cares.” This is, as another person pointed out, “just how the gay world works.” Even if the straights were a little bit scandalized, as one friend of his — who added that they shared an ex — said, “It wasn’t anything that crazy to the gays. He doesn’t have a bad bone in his body. Did you know he used to bartend on Fire Island?”

On the trail, his campaign manager insists everything’s been just as easygoing. “We rarely get asked about it. The first event that we had after everything, we go in and not a single person asked about it. Maybe the real world is not the internet.” Somewhat shockingly, his opponent still hasn’t commented on the photographs. Gallant mostly seems pleased to be getting this much attention. He has taken to calling this his “Kim Kardashian moment” and told the New York Times unabashedly that he’s “kinky as fuck.”

But how gay can a politician really be, especially in a solidly Republican district? Voters may accept a squeaky-clean, wonkish Pete Buttigieg type, who met his husband, supposedly, on Hinge and is a proudly devoted father. But could they ever accept a proudly kinky gay like Gallant? Even after several drinks at Almond, Gallant seemed to know the limits — that simply turning out a bunch of turned-on gay guys won’t win him the election. Though his campaign had given me the impression he was ready to “lean in” to his new reputation — sharing tweets from gays on the internet crowing about “sexual liberation” and unashamed “sexual deviancy” — and assured me that Gallant would answer any question I wanted, he mostly sidestepped anything too naughty. Could constituents handle a congressman on Grindr, I asked him? “Why not?” he said, before noting that he wouldn’t personally because he’s in a “very good relationship” with his fiancé. What about those kinks? “Oh, God. That’s a deep question. Um … I can’t put that on the record. I’m happy to tell you, but it’s not on the record,” he said. Eventually, he came up with a voter-friendly answer, one that might actually appeal in this district. “My biggest turn-on is to have a man who knows what he wants.” Was he ever a go-go boy? He declined to say. Rather, he insisted he doesn’t even go out that much anymore. “In my jobs, I have to be very straitlaced,” he said. “I can’t do drugs. I have to be very clean, all that stuff. I don’t usually drink that much. I enjoy a glass of wine every now and then, a cocktail here and there. The reality is I’m too busy.”

The week after we met, his campaign put out a new ad, where he was back to flying helicopters, grilling brats, and rocking a pair of aviators in a fire truck, all the while talking about grocery prices and backing the police. By then, Decision Desk HQ had his chances of winning the race at 30 percent, up two points since the nude leak; when the FEC released the latest campaign filings this week, Gallant had outraised LaLota for the first time, by nearly half a million dollars. Gallant is wondering if it all might have been worth it. “I always complained my name recognition wasn’t enough,” he’d told me at Almond, just as we were interrupted by a fan looking to take a photo. “Now, it’s, you know, it’s there.”

Early clinical trials into a new fat reduction treatment have reported promising results, and the treatment takes a more unusual approach: Rather than shrinking fat cells, as most weight loss strategies do, it safely and naturally kills them off.

The drug here is CBL-514, which is administered via injection. As well as proving effective at reducing subcutaneous fat (just below the skin), there's evidence it can also reduce visceral fat (stored deeper around the organs).

According to the team behind the trials, CBL-514 and its unconventional strategy have the potential to reduce fat in key areas of the body – with further benefits that come with weight loss likely to follow.

"We expect that patients will be pleased by the cosmetic effects, such as the flatter stomach that can come with subcutaneous fat loss," says endocrinologist Timothy Garvey, from the University of Alabama at Birmingham, who headed up the trial.
"But it is the reduction in body weight, loss of visceral fat and the improvements in blood pressure, cholesterol and the like that should be associated with this that will be important for health."

To be clear, these results haven't been peer-reviewed yet – they're from a conference presentation and company announcements, not a published study, so they should be taken with a grain of salt for now.

There are several different components to the research. Two phase 2 clinical trials, CBL-0204 and CBL-0205, involved 107 and 173 participants respectively, and showed that CBL-514 was effective at reducing subcutaneous fat in the majority of the volunteers.
Since those trials were carried out, the records of a subset of 41 participants have been analyzed for changes in visceral fat too.

Those given CBL-514 injections for up to 12 weeks showed an average reduction of 12.01 percent in visceral fat, while those on a placebo treatment averaged a visceral fat increase of 5.68 percent four weeks after their final injection.

"These results provide encouraging early evidence that CBL-514 can reduce visceral-fat volume in the abdominal region," says epidemiologist Marie Spreckley, from the University of Cambridge in the UK, who wasn't involved in the research.
"Larger trials with longer follow-up will be important to establish whether the fat reduction lasts and whether it leads to improvements in health."

The final part of the picture so far comes from animal tests. Rats treated with the GLP-1 drug tirzepatide and CBL-514 together lost more weight on average than rats who were given doses of tirzepatide on its own.
What's more, the rats given both medications gained less weight when the tirzepatide treatment was stopped.

GLP-1 drugs like tirzepatide are commonly prescribed for type 2 diabetes and weight loss, and are named after the glucagon-like peptide-1 they're designed to mimic. While they can be very effective, any lost weight often returns after a GLP-1 course has finished.

It's possible that the way CBL-514 causes fat cells to self-destruct (technically known as apoptosis) means it's then more difficult for the pounds to pile back on – but this part of the research needs to be investigated further in tests on people, while other effects of the treatment are also assessed.

"To be a useful obesity therapy it will be critical to show that this doesn't increase the risk of fat accumulation in other organs or poorer control of blood fat and sugar levels," says metabolism researcher Justin Rochford, from the University of Aberdeen in the UK, who wasn't involved in the research.
The researchers are now working towards larger trials with bigger groups of participants tracked over a longer time period, which will assess how the losses in fat might impact overall health.

CBL-514 was originally developed to remove fatty lumps under the skin called lipomas, and so far, the signs are promising that the drug's targeted fat cell removal technique could be valuable much more broadly.
"This is a highly innovative approach to obesity pharmacotherapy that has produced some remarkable results in early human trials," says Garvey.

A U.S. Air Force F-22 pilot controlled a YFQ-44A Fury Collaborative Combat Aircraft this month while both aircraft were in flight, according to an Oct. 16 release, another milestone in the service’s ambitious CCA efforts.

The human F-22 pilot acted as an “airborne quarterback” for the YFQ-44 drone by sending it high-level tactical directives, according to the Air Force statement. The YFQ-44’s on-board autonomy software then interpreted and carried out those orders in real time to carry out “dynamic flight maneuvers and simulated combat tasks,” the statement reads.
Anduril Industries, the manufacturer of the Fury, said in follow-up statements that the flight took place out of Edwards Air Force Base, Calif., during the week of Oct. 5.

Mark Shushnar, Anduril’s vice president of autonomous airpower, said the Fury and F-22 both took off at Edwards, and then joined up midair. The Raptor pilot then sent an updated mission plan to the Fury CCA using a tactical data link, “commanding Fury through operationally relevant maneuvers from the cockpit of the crewed quarterback” fighter.

For this demonstration, the F-22 was controlling a single YFQ-44A. But the Air Force’s plan is to eventually have each fighter pilot capable of controlling multiple CCAs as a formation—extending the service’s combat mass and reach.

In a statement, Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Kenneth S. Wilsbach said the demo “shows the power of crewed-uncrewed teaming and the advantage it provides our warfighters” and pledged to build on it quickly.
“We must test often, learn fast, and give commanders what they need, when they need it,” he said.
Air Force Secretary Troy Meink also touted the need to move quickly in touting the flight.

“This achievement demonstrates what is possible when we are aligned with industry on a shared imperative: delivering capability to the warfighter at unprecedented speed,” Meink said in a statement. “We are driving urgency into every part of acquisition from rapid integration and flight learning to disciplined assessment, so we can turn promising technology into combat capability at the pace the threat demands.”
The mission lasted multiple hours and was a success, Shushnar said, and shows how quickly progress is being made to creating an operational CCA program.

“The U.S. Air Force’s CCA program is the fastest moving, most mature CCA program anywhere in the world, and will be the first to field operational aircraft,” Shushnar said. “Getting there demands that Anduril and the U.S. Air Force work together to prove out the capability, define the operational procedures, and build trust between operators and their semi-autonomous wingmen.”
The Air Force said data from the test will help with future software integration, developmental testing, and future CCA concepts.

The test included personnel from the Air Force’s 412th Test Wing at Edwards, the 422nd Test and Evaluation Squadron at Nellis Air Force Base, Nev., the 309th Software Engineering Group at Hill Air Force Base, Utah, the CCA Experimental Operations Unit at Creech Air Force Base, Nev., the F-22 System Program Office, and the CCA Software Autonomy and Teaming Branch.

The Air Force has previously conducted flight tests with a “surrogate” drone meant to represent a CCA—General Atomics’ MQ-20 Avenger. In February, an F-22 in the air controlled an MQ-20 Avenger, and in May, an F-35 that remained on the ground also controlled an Avenger that was in the air.

The Air Force wants to have 500 CCAs in the field by 2032, and eventually a fleet of 1,000 or more to carry out a variety of missions that could include air-to-air strikes, air-to-ground strikes, intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, or electronic warfare. This first iteration—which includes General Atomics’ FQ-42 and Anduril’s FQ-44—is focused on the air-to-air mission. The Air Force wants them to cost at most $20 million apiece for the air vehicle, excluding the cost of sensors, weapons or other equipment CCAs might carry on board.

While the focus of the CCA program has been on manned-unmanned teaming with pilots in the air, the Air Force has also been working on a capability for Airmen to command the CCAs using stations on the ground.

NASA’s Deep Space Network facility in California is marking the addition of a brand new 34-meter-wide (114-foot-wide) radio frequency antenna to the agency’s deep space communications and navigation system. The network uses giant dish antennas located at three global facilities to support more than 40 spacecraft exploring the solar system and interstellar space.
The new Deep Space Station 23 (DSS-23) is located at the Goldstone Deep Space Communications Complex, near Barstow, and is managed by NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California.

NASA leadership and personnel as well as dignitaries gathered at the complete DSS-23 antenna for a ceremonial ribbon cutting. It’s the latest to be added as part of the Deep Space Network’s Aperture Enhancement Project, which began in 2009 to upgrade and expand the network by adding six new 34-meter multifrequency beam-waveguide antennas. These versatile dishes can enhance many missions operating over different radio frequencies.

“By expanding the Deep Space Network, we are strengthening the communications foundation NASA needs for the bold missions ahead — from exploring more of the Moon than ever before to peering deeper into the solar system,” said James Kenyon, associate administrator of the Research and Technology Mission Directorate at NASA Headquarters in Washington. “This new antenna will help us deliver on our national goals for space exploration and push beyond the limits of what once seemed impossible.”

After completing a testing campaign from May through July to demonstrate its capabilities, the new DSS-23 began operations on Aug. 3, tracking NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory. Since then, it has been communicating with dozens of missions such as NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, Psyche, Juno, Voyager 1, and other robotic spacecraft in deep space.

“The addition of this next-generation antenna brings us closer to a completely modernized network that embraces advanced technology to ensure NASA’s leadership in deep space communications,” said Dave Gallagher, director of JPL. “After over 60 years of continuous operations supporting consequential missions, these upgrades prime the network for a new era of exploration. The teams that designed, planned, and built DSS-23 should be proud.”

Construction of DSS-23 began in February 2020. After the 133-ton metal reflector framework was placed and bolted atop the antenna’s pedestal in December 2024, engineers installed the panels to the framework that reflect radio frequency signals transmitted to and received from spacecraft. Then came the careful process of calibrating the antenna so it can work in concert with the rest of the network.

It is the fifth antenna at Goldstone (joining three 34-meter antennas and one 70-meter, or 230-foot, antenna) and the fifth enhancement project antenna to join the network, which includes antennas at the DSN’s Goldstone, Madrid, and Canberra, Australia, complexes. Multifrequency beam waveguide antennas direct signals down to a stable, climate-controlled underground room, rather than housing heavy, sensitive electronic equipment on the moving antenna dish. In addition to offering versatility, this design allows easy access for maintenance and upgrades to the system.

“The biggest challenge wasn’t actually constructing the antenna. It was transforming a complex collection of mechanical, electrical, software, radio frequency, and infrastructure systems into a single, mission-ready asset,” said Germaine Aziz, manager of the Deep Space Network Aperture Enhancement Project at JPL. “Every subsystem must be integrated, calibrated, and verified to operate with extraordinary precision and reliability before it can support NASA’s deep space missions.”

The enhancement project will be complete when a sixth enhancement-project antenna, Deep Space Station 33, comes online at the Canberra facility in 2029, bringing the total number of 34-meter antennas across the network to 13. The 34-meter antennas can be arrayed (combined and operated together) to provide an equivalent communications backup for each facility’s single 70-meter antenna, which, after more than 50 years of near-continuous operation, are getting increasingly costly to maintain and repair.

Managed by Caltech for NASA, JPL manages the agency’s Deep Space Network with the oversight of NASA’s SCaN (Space Communications and Navigation) Program within NASA’s Research and Technology Mission Directorate. More than 100 NASA and non-NASA missions rely on the Deep Space Network and Near Space Network. They include missions that support astronauts aboard the International Space Station and future Artemis missions, monitoring Earth, exploring the Moon, and exploring the solar system and beyond.

From the International Space Station’s unique position 250 miles above Earth, the Sun is a vital source of energy. Solar power supports the station’s life support systems, daily activities, and hundreds of research investigations that improve life on Earth and prepare humans for deep space exploration. Over the past five years, NASA augmented the station’s power generation and distribution capability with next-generation International Space Station Roll Out Solar Arrays (IROSAs).

In 2017, a technology demonstration conducted aboard the space station tested the effectiveness of the arrays. The lightweight, compact design launches as a cylinder and unfurls like a yoga mat after installation. This advanced design reduces mass and volume at launch and uses an autonomous, self-deploying system that minimizes risks during rollout.

The IROSAs were designed, manufactured, and tested by Redwire under a contract with Boeing and are about half the size of the station’s legacy arrays. Despite being smaller, the arrays are capable of producing about 28 kilowatts of additional power.

Six IROSAs were installed outside of the space station between 2021 and 2023. In 2023, power projections prompted a request for another set of IROSAs, which launched in Dragon spacecraft’s trunk during the SpaceX 35th commercial resupply services mission to space station for NASA. Together, the eight IROSAs will increase power by more than 160kW for research and operations.

With the full upgrade in place, the space station’s revitalized power system not only supports NASA’s legacy in low Earth orbit but also helps advance technology that will extend the agency’s reach into the solar system. From planetary defense demonstrations, like the Double Asteroid Redirection Test, to future human exploration efforts, the space station is an essential testbed for the technologies needed for expeditions beyond Earth’s orbit.

On the evening of 8 September 1930, the German mathematician David Hilbert stepped up to a microphone in Königsberg and addressed his countrymen by radio. He was 68, recently retired, and at the height of his fame. The talk was a defence of pure reason, delivered in the city of Immanuel Kant, and it ended with two phrases that would later be carved on his tombstone: Wir müssen wissen. Wir werden wissen. We must know. We shall know.

Are certain questions closed to the human mind? Are there truths about the world that we can never know? Hilbert thought that, at least within mathematics, this could not be the case. For him, mathematics was a game played with symbols: one could fix the right axioms as rules of the game and every mathematical problem could be solved. He was wrong.

The day before his Königsberg address, at a small academic meeting in the same city, a 24-year-old Austrian named Kurt Gödel had quietly announced that no such system for arithmetic could exist. Whatever reasonable set of rules you fix, something true must lie beyond them and thus beyond our knowledge. We can’t know. We won’t know. Gödel’s results, known as the Incompleteness Theorems, are landmark achievements of 20th-century logic. Recent work in philosophy and mathematics has begun to illuminate the gap they opened, and with it something deeper about the foundations of knowledge itself. The story begins in the same city, but two centuries earlier.

When Kant remembered a book by David Hume he’d read years earlier, he was woken from what he called his ‘dogmatic slumber’. Kant had believed that pure reasoning could teach us every absolute truth about the world, but Hume had asked a question that that stumped him: what reason do we actually have to believe that the future will resemble the past? We may have seen the Sun rise a thousand times, but how do we know it will rise tomorrow? The belief that the future will resemble the past is, Hume argued, merely a kind of habit. Kant couldn’t answer Hume’s challenge and was silenced for a decade.
For Hume, proving a theorem was like unpacking a suitcase to find an outfit. Kant could not leave it there

When Kant finally broke his silence with the Critique of Pure Reason (1781), he offered a radical answer. We can know the world only as it appears to our minds, and that is where our science sits; the noumenal world – the Ding an sich (the ‘thing-in-itself’) – simply lies beyond our reach. Causation is not something we discover in the world, but something the mind supplies for experience to be coherent at all. When we watch a cat push a glass off a table, we don’t see a bare sequence of motions and then infer, by some metaphysical principle, that the push caused the fall. No: we see the push as causing the fall. The causal structure is not a hypothesis we add to the experience; it is part of how the experience comes to us in the first place. It is in our minds already.

So far, so good: Kant has met Hume’s challenge, and the workings of science are intelligible: we are structuring our experiences. But the work is not done, for there remains mathematics, the very language in which the sciences are framed. Hume was content that arithmetic and algebra are merely the unpacking of definitions; that proving a theorem is like unpacking a suitcase to find an outfit. Kant could not leave it there. If mathematics were only such unpacking, how could it underwrite the sciences? Either the sciences tell us nothing new about the world, or something has gone missing from the account.

Does one unpack ‘add 7 and 5’ to find ‘12’? Kant thought not. Rather, one constructs 12 from 7 and 5 in the mind. More than a century later, a young Dutch mathematician called L E J Brouwer, following Kant’s thought, argued that, if the mathematician’s work consists in such mental constructions, then one cannot assume any statement is either true or false. That was controversial: to strip the mathematician of that assumption, Hilbert retorted, would be like ‘proscribing … to the boxer the use of his fists’.

Gottlob Frege, working in the late 19th century, found Kant’s account of mathematics intolerable for different reasons: arithmetic, he claimed, is not psychological. The numbers exist whether anyone counts them or not. He set about reducing arithmetic to pure logic, grounded in the mind-independent categories of True and False. The project consumed two decades of his life and produced some of the most consequential advances in the philosophy of language and mathematics in history. It is widely regarded as having sparked the modern discipline of logic. And yet, as the second volume of his masterwork, the Grundgesetze der Arithmetik, sat at the printer in 1902, the foundations cracked. The British philosopher Bertrand Russell sent Frege a letter pointing out an inconsistency at the heart of the system. A melancholy note in his diary later summed up his defeat: ‘My efforts to become clear about what is meant by number have resulted in failure.’

Russell had been wrestling with the foundations of mathematics for some years before his letter. It was only after meeting the Italian mathematician Giuseppe Peano at the International Congress of Philosophy in 1900 that he acquired the tools to attempt the problem. In place of Frege’s edifice, Russell set out to build his own, together with his colleague Alfred North Whitehead. Principia Mathematica appeared in three massive volumes between 1910 and 1913: all of mathematics, grounded in pure logic.
Mathematics carries what’s already there without adding anything, as plumbing moves water without supplying any

Russell’s student Ludwig Wittgenstein spent the war in the Austro-Hungarian artillery, volunteering again and again for the most exposed posts he could find – an observation position under fire on the Eastern Front, from which he was decorated for bravery at least three times. He carried notebooks. In them, between bombardments, he worked the Frege-Russell philosophy into a complete account of how language touches the world: the world is made of facts, a sentence is a picture of a fact, and whatever can be said at all can be said clearly. He finished the manuscript in an Italian prisoner-of-war camp in 1918 and sent it to Russell from the camp. Wittgenstein took himself to have solved the problems of philosophy, gave away his inherited fortune, and left to teach primary school in the Austrian mountains.

The Tractatus became the manifesto of a group of philosophers in Vienna including Moritz Schlick, Rudolf Carnap and Otto Neurath, who called their position logical positivism. A statement is meaningful only if there is some way of settling whether it is true. Analytic statements are settled by unfolding the definitions of the words involved: for example, ‘All bachelors are unmarried’ is true because a bachelor is, by definition, an unmarried man. Synthetic statements are claims about the world, and are settled by – in principle – going out and looking: ‘It rained in Vienna on 3 June 1929’ is false because one could have observed that the sky over the Ringstrasse stayed clear that day. Anything else is grammar without content.

The Vienna Circle, as they became known, claimed that mathematics is analytic and science is synthetic. The function of mathematics is to extract information from scientific claims: it carries what is already there without adding anything, the way plumbing moves water without supplying any. If the Vienna Circle were right, then Kant’s and Brouwer’s restrictions on scientific and mathematical knowledge were entirely unnecessary. If.

By 1929, after almost three decades of labours by Hilbert, Russell, Frege, Wittgenstein, the Vienna Circle and Brouwer, among others, the foundations of mathematics looked very nearly finished. One beam remained that would lock the whole frame together. In the plenary addresses for the International Congress of Mathematicians in Paris in 1900, Hilbert had set out 23 problems that would define the next century of the subject. The second problem was this: prove that arithmetic is consistent – that is, no chain of reasoning from the axioms, however long, would yield a contradiction. The beam would not go in.

While studying physics at the University of Vienna in the 1920s, Gödel had attended Schlick’s seminar on Russell, which drew him into the problems of logic and, by way of them, into Hilbert’s programme. His PhD in 1929 showed that the standard system of first-order logic is complete – every logically valid statement can, in principle, be derived from the axioms of logic. It was the result Hilbert wanted, though for pure logic rather than mathematics. A year later, he turned to the natural next step: the consistency of arithmetic, Hilbert’s second problem.

What he announced at the Königsberg meeting the day before Hilbert’s radio address, no one had expected. Taking Principia Mathematica as the articulation of mathematics within logic, Gödel showed that there were true mathematical statements that cannot be proved using the resources of Principia Mathematica alone. Among them is the statement ‘Principia Mathematica is consistent.’ The trick at the heart of the proof is to encode statements about the system within the system itself – a move with the same vertiginous quality as Russell’s letter to Frege. But where Russell’s letter had killed a system, Gödel’s theorem killed a programme.
The one-time prophet of the Vienna Circle left nothing of its philosophy standing
His argument was so general that it applied to any reasonable system for arithmetic. Hilbert’s dream of an axiomatic system capturing all of mathematics – or even just arithmetic – was over.

The response in Vienna was disbelief, then dismay. The Circle had built its philosophy on the assumption that mathematics was analytic; Gödel had shown it wasn’t as simple as that. Carnap struggled for years to absorb the result. Wittgenstein dismissed it, but was already repudiating the Tractatus himself. Meaning, he came to argue, lay not in matching picture to reality but simply in how people discourse in public. The one-time prophet of the Circle left nothing of its philosophy standing.

Hilbert never publicly conceded that Gödel’s result doomed his programme. He died in 1943; his colleagues had by then been murdered or exiled by the Nazis. His tombstone in Göttingen bears the words he had spoken into the Königsberg microphone: Wir müssen wissen. Wir werden wissen. We must know. We shall know.

And Gödel? After the Anschluss, he escaped Vienna for Princeton, where he continued to make extraordinary contributions to logic while taking long walks with his close friend Albert Einstein. At his American citizenship exam in 1947, asked by the judge whether a regime like the Nazis’ could arise in the United States, he began to explain a logical loophole he had found in the Constitution that would permit exactly that. The judge cut him off and moved the proceedings swiftly to their conclusion. (We still don’t know what loophole he found.)

The orthodox response was to keep the truth and give up the proof. There is a realm of mathematical fact, standing independent of us, and axiomatic systems reach only part of it; incompleteness measures the distance between what is so and what we can show. Its most committed advocate was Gödel himself. However, two problems come with the realm. First, with logical positivism in ruins, Kant’s problem returns: if mathematical truth is independent of the mind, how can it structure sciences that exist within the mind? Second, the realm is posited chiefly to spare us two unwelcome alternatives – psychologism on one side, Brouwer’s restrictions on the other. Avoiding two conclusions is not an argument for a third.

In 1973, the British philosopher Michael Dummett was invited to deliver the annual philosophical lecture at the British Academy. He took as his subject ‘The Justification of Deduction’ – how to justify the ordinary practices of mathematicians without helping oneself to the assumption that their subject matter exists in a realm of its own. The problem, he told his audience, was perhaps ‘one of the most fundamental and intractable problems … in all philosophy’.

Dummett was the great Frege scholar of the 20th century; his Frege: Philosophy of Language (1973) brought an otherwise obscure figure to the forefront of the discipline. The book had been years in the writing, but in 1964, with the manuscript all but finished, Dummett put down his pen. He conceived it his duty, he explains in the preface, to involve himself ‘actively in opposition to the racism which was becoming more and more manifest in English life.’ When he returned to the manuscript several years later, a previously suppressed fragment of Frege’s Nachlass (ie, his literary estate) had surfaced, revealing the philosopher as a ‘virulent racist’ with ‘extreme Right-wing political opinions’. Once his book was finally published, Dummett recorded the bitter irony, and reflected that he had learned something dark about how a mind he revered could harbour views he despised.
Our linguistic practices – the ways in which we are prepared to assert, justify and infer – determine logic

What Dummett took from Frege’s work on logic was that the problems of mathematics are, at heart, problems of language. Where things had gone wrong, he thought, was that Frege had grounded his account in a mind-independent notion of truth. ‘In this respect (and in this respect alone),’ Dummett wrote, ‘Frege’s new approach to logic was retrograde.’ For Frege, logic answered to truth: the rules were good because they preserved something already fixed. Dummett turned this around.

Following Wittgenstein’s later thinking, Dummett argued ‘a theory of meaning is a theory of understanding.’ And understanding, he insisted, must be manifestable: whatever a competent speaker knows in knowing what a sentence means must be something she can, in principle, display in her use of language. In The Logical Basis of Metaphysics (1991), Dummett gave this account of language, logic and reality its most sustained form. Our linguistic practices – the ways in which we are prepared to assert, justify and infer – determine logic. Logic, in turn, determines what counts as a fact, what counts as truth, and ultimately what we are entitled to regard as real.

Consider how a child learns the word ‘red’. We do not begin by telling her about light of a certain wavelength, or the metaphysics of colour properties, or the conditions that would make ‘this is red’ true. We point at things. We correct her when she calls a ripe tomato green; we approve when she calls a fire engine red. Over time, she comes to use the word as we do – and at that point, she understands it. There is no further fact, hidden behind the practice, in which her understanding consists. The understanding is the practice, competently exercised.

Dummett died in 2011, having been knighted in 1999 for ‘services to philosophy and to racial justice’. He is remembered as one of the most significant British philosophers of the previous century. Yet for all its power, his programme remained a prospectus: he set out what a theory of language, logic and reality must achieve, but he never completed one.

In 2005, Tor Sandqvist, a doctoral student at Uppsala University, submitted a thesis that took up Dummett’s challenge: to justify the ordinary practices of mathematicians without any appeal to truth. Where Dummett had given the conditions a solution must satisfy, Sandqvist gave a solution. He produced a precise mathematical justification of deduction as mathematicians actually use it, grounded entirely in practices of assertion. The boxer’s fists were untied.

It was rediscovered a decade later in the Department of Computer Science at University College London, where a group of logicians recognised what Sandqvist had actually built, and developed it into a full framework on a par with the orthodox truth-conditional view. The framework now stands equal to the truth-based account, analogous to the situation after Gödel’s PhD thesis. What about mathematics? The UCL team have recently shown that the Dummett-Sandqvist framework gives a way to understand what Gödel’s Incompleteness Theorems are about, and it is not the limits of knowledge.

If meaning comes from practices of assertion, then our concepts are settled only as far as our practices have settled them. A system of definitions is a kind of constitution that determines something. The US Constitution, for example, is meant to enshrine a form of democracy. But what a constitution defines answers to how it is amended.
An amendment can betray what a constitution defines. But it can also unfold it

Principia Mathematica is a constitution for arithmetic. To read it as a constitution is to assume it is consistent; otherwise, it would be nonsense. So, when we amend it by asserting that ‘Principia Mathematica is consistent,’ we are not changing the subject: the new axiom says aloud only what the practice already did. Gödel’s theorems apply afresh to the enlarged constitution: the amended system has its own unprovable truth, its own consistency it cannot certify. No amendment is the last; each faithful extension opens room for the next. To grasp a concept like arithmetic is not to survey a finished structure; it is to hold a principle for going on: a rule for laying the next stretch of line, not a map of where the line ends. Dummett called this openness indefinite extensibility.

Faithful is the word doing the work, because not every amendment is. Gödel claimed the US Constitution could deliver a dictatorship. That does not make dictatorship a form of democracy. Whatever loophole he had in mind, it would have contradicted the practices the Constitution already enshrined. An amendment can betray what a constitution defines. But it can also unfold it, drawing out what the founding commitments demanded all along. Only the second kind is what Dummett has in mind.

The constitution of our language is our current practice for public discourse. As it is extensible in this way, what we claim as ‘true’ is not a fixed structure with a ceiling we are forever failing to reach, but something that can change. Gödel’s verdict never applied to mathematics, but only to some edition of the constitution. Within the Sandqvist system, we can attend to the extension systematically. Hilbert’s words outlive his programme: Wir werden wissen. We shall know. Not because the answers are waiting at the end of a ladder, but because truth goes exactly as far as we have built the rungs.
Eminem defended his guest verse on Kid Rock’s new faith-based album, saying their long friendship overshadowed their political divide.
Rock released his new LP Halfway 2 Jesus on Friday, with Slim Shady — a fellow Detroit native and longtime friend of the rocker — appearing on the track “Heal My Faith.”

The collaboration drew some criticism from some of Eminem’s fans who were taken aback that the rapper — who publicly endorsed Kamala Harris at a Detroit rally in 2024 and has been critical of Trump on tracks like “Campaign Speech” — could collaborate with Kid Rock, perhaps Trump’s biggest (and most relevant) supporter in the music industry.
As Eminem explained on social media hours after Halfway 2 Jesus was released, “Not about choosing sides, just choosing to make music with my old friend. Praying for all of us.”

Kid Rock elaborated on the collaboration in an interview with Billboard, revealing that while Eminem was first announced as a guest on the song “7 Sins,” the rapper instead appeared on “Heal My Faith,” the song Rock initially recruited him for. “We agreed we didn’t need two songs together…people are going to think we’re dating,” Rock said.

“We’ve been friends for, like, 40 years. I really didn’t want to drag him into my political world…. We talk about [politics] a little bit, not a ton. There’s a lot of stuff we agree on, and we can have a laugh about what [we don’t]. That’s why I asked him to write a verse for me.”

“From shock rap to the rock rap / My homie and me /He is my brother, not my political enemy,” Eminem raps on his verse. “B.O. to the B. / We wrote this for those who believe in G.O. to the D / However you voted or lean / Liberal and evangelical can agree / It’s God first, home of the free.”

“This [album] is about forgiveness and second chances,” Rock told Billboard. “Trying to heal some of the division in our country. I’m just putting a positive message out there in the world… showing a little more grace, trying to kill some of the division.”

Quentin Tarantino has long said he’ll be retiring after his 10th feature film, but fans shouldn’t worry yet. While the “Pulp Fiction” director confirmed he’d finished penning the script for his final project, he won’t be getting much further with it until his newly opened play, “The Popinjay Cavalier,” closes.

Tarantino made the statement on a recent episode of “The Graham Norton Show,” where he joined the host alongside fellow guests Ellen DeGeneres, Colin Farrell and Gemma Chan. It was his first appearance on the show in more than a decade.

“I’ve written a script that I really like, but I want to do the play and see who I am; then I’ll then go back and spend time with my family and live a little and then see what I want to do,” Tarantino said.

He also gave audiences more insight into “The Popinjay Cavalier,” which he said started as a screenplay before the director realized “it really worked as a play.” “I think it will be thrilling,” he said.

Starring Sacha Baron Cohen, “The Popinjay Cavalier” will open at London’s Phoenix Theatre next March, following previews in late Feb. The play, described as a “swashbuckling comedy,” is set to run for three months, closing on June 13. “I’m keen with anticipation to give the West End a great night out,” Tarantino said in a statement when the show was announced.

Tarantino’s most recent release remains “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood,” which came out in 2019 and starred Brad Pitt, Leonardo DiCaprio, Margot Robbie, Margaret Qualley and more. Pitt won the Oscar for best supporting actor that year, as did Barbara Ling and Nancy Haigh for best production design. Tarantino was also nominated for best picture and best director, while DiCaprio was nominated for best actor.
Brain cells meant to protect us may be fueling cognitive decline

- Scientists have uncovered a surprising cause of age-related cognitive decline involving brain cells previously thought to be entirely beneficial. As these cells become dysfunctional, they can produce abnormal amounts of myelin, disrupting nerve fibers and potentially contributing to worsening memory and thinking skills.

Brain cells that normally help protect the brain may play an unexpected role in cognitive decline as we grow older. Scientists have discovered that cells responsible for maintaining the protective coating around nerve fibers can become dysfunctional with age, potentially contributing to the gradual loss of memory and thinking abilities.

The research, published in Nature Medicine, challenges the long-held belief that these cells are always beneficial. By examining human brain tissue and conducting experiments in mice, researchers found evidence that problems with these normally supportive cells can damage nerve fibers and interfere with cognitive function.

The discovery also points to a possible new approach for protecting the aging brain. Drugs that act on the biological pathway involved are already being used to treat other neurological conditions, raising hopes that existing treatments could eventually be adapted to combat age-related cognitive decline.
Scientists Discover Changes in the Aging Brain

The study was led by researchers from the University of Edinburgh and the UK Dementia Research Institute, who investigated how changes in the brain relate to declining cognitive abilities later in life.

Their research focused on the Lothian Birth Cohort 1936, a group of people whose cognitive abilities have been tracked from childhood into old age. This unusually extensive record allowed scientists to investigate how thinking and memory changed over decades.
Between ages 70 and 82, participants underwent assessments measuring memory, the speed at which they processed information, and their ability to understand spatial relationships.

Of the 1,091 people enrolled in the cohort, 866 completed additional cognitive testing after age 70. Nearly everyone experienced at least some decline, but the rate varied considerably. These differences gave researchers an opportunity to investigate what might distinguish brains experiencing faster deterioration from those aging more gradually.

When scientists examined brain tissue collected after death from a subset of participants, they discovered a striking pattern. Individuals who had experienced greater cognitive decline tended to have fewer large nerve fibers, along with an abnormal buildup of unhealthy myelin.

Myelin is the protective coating that surrounds nerve fibers, helping electrical signals travel efficiently through the brain. Although this insulation is essential for normal brain function, the findings suggest that excessive or abnormal myelin may become part of the problem.

The changes were especially pronounced around the large nerve fibers that remained. Importantly, these abnormalities were associated with how quickly cognitive abilities declined, rather than how well someone performed on cognitive tests at a particular age.
A Protective Brain Cell May Have a Hidden Weakness
To understand what might be causing these changes, the researchers turned their attention to oligodendrocytes, specialized brain cells responsible for producing and maintaining myelin.

Oligodendrocytes have traditionally been regarded as beneficial because they help keep nerve fibers insulated and functioning properly. However, the new findings suggest that these cells can become dysfunctional during aging and may contribute to the very problems they normally help prevent.
The researchers discovered that people with more severe cognitive decline had lower levels of a protein called NRF2 inside their oligodendrocytes.

NRF2 plays an important protective role in cells by regulating hundreds of genes involved in defending against damage and maintaining normal cellular function. When its activity decreases, cells may become less capable of protecting themselves and performing their usual jobs.
To investigate whether this protein was directly involved in the brain changes, the team conducted experiments in mice.

When researchers specifically reduced NRF2 in oligodendrocytes, the animals developed excessive myelin and lost large nerve fibers, closely resembling the abnormalities observed in human brain tissue. The mice also showed reduced improvements in cognitive performance as they aged.

These experiments provided evidence that declining NRF2 activity can directly disrupt oligodendrocyte function, potentially triggering changes in myelin and nerve fibers that contribute to cognitive decline.
Existing Drugs Could Offer a New Treatment Strategy
The findings may have important implications for developing treatments that help preserve cognitive abilities in older adults.
One particularly promising aspect is that the NRF2 pathway is already a target of medications used for other conditions, including a drug prescribed to treat multiple sclerosis (MS).

Previous studies have found that increasing NRF2 activity can improve cognitive function in people with MS. That raises the possibility that medications acting on the same pathway might eventually be repurposed to address oligodendrocyte dysfunction and age-related cognitive decline.
Although further research is needed to determine whether such treatments would benefit older adults experiencing cognitive decline, the discovery identifies a potentially valuable therapeutic target.
Veronique Miron, MRC Senior Non-Clinical Fellow and UK Dementia Research Institute Group Leader at the University of Edinburgh and St. Michael's Hospital, part of Unity Health Toronto, said:

"As the prevalence of cognitive decline is rising with an aging population and no current treatments exist, we are excited about this work as it points to a potential strategy for new therapeutic strategies to preserve cognitive ability in aging."
A New Understanding of Cognitive Decline
Beyond its potential medical applications, the research changes how scientists understand the role of oligodendrocytes in the aging brain.
Rather than simply providing support for healthy nerve function throughout life, these cells appear capable of becoming dysfunctional and contributing to cognitive problems.
Georgina Craig, the study's first author and a Postdoctoral Fellow at St Michael's Hospital in Toronto and the UK Dementia Research Institute, said:

"This study has fundamentally shifted how we think about these brain cells in aging. We have always considered oligodendrocytes as purely beneficial, yet here we surprisingly find that they can become dysfunctional and contribute to cognitive impairment in aging."
The findings suggest that maintaining healthy oligodendrocyte function could become an important strategy for protecting memory and thinking abilities as people grow older.
