Georgia picked a bad time to play its worst game of the season on Saturday afternoon against Auburn.

The Bulldogs allowed a blocked field goal, turned it over three times and committed a couple of critical penalties contributing directly to the Tigers' stunning 27-24 victory. The Auburn win snaps Georgia's 54-game winning streak against unranked competition.

Georgia committed three personal fouls against Auburn quarterback Byrum Brown, including one in the final seconds that put the Tigers in position for Alex McPherson's game-winning field goal as time expired.

Smart said before the game he was worried about Auburn's physicality and his team being banged up coming off last week's win at Alabama, and it showed as the Tigers borrowed from the Bulldogs' playbook by winning at the line of scrimmage.

Georgia led 14-0 before Auburn scored the game's next 24 points to take a 24-14 lead into the fourth quarter. The Tigers' victory was their first over a ranked opponent since 2021 and marked their first win over a top-ranked foe since doing it twice during the 2017 campaign.

On a critical 3rd-and-11 with 1:16 to play at its own 29-yard line, Auburn had a bad snap, resulting in an immediate punt and giving Georgia a potential game-winning possession. However, Stockton lost a fumble near midfield with 58 seconds left to put the Tigers in business with all three timeouts.
Georgia had won nine straight against Auburn dating back to 2017 and it was only Smart's second rivalry loss against the Tigers in 12 tries.
Georgia was previously 41-4 when ranked No. 1 under Smart, including an 18-0 at home.
A teary-eyed Auburn coach Alex Golesh tried to put words with his emotions after his first signature win for the Tigers in his first season as the leader of the program.

"(Golesh's son) Bear said Thursday, 'Dad, can I get on the field after we win' … you're on the field bro,," Golesh said. "I'm just grateful for our guys. You can have so many narratives and stories … I'm just grateful for our guys, our coaches, our fan base … it's been through a lot. We're going to build Auburn back to where everybody wants it. One game at a time. Just hang with us."
Golesh said he received texts before the game from Auburn legends Takeo Spikes and Jason Campbell, among others, reminding him that he is the right man for the job.
Auburn suspended their top defensive player, Xavier Atkins, for Saturday's game, but managed to put together one of its most complete performances of the season on that side of the football.

Stockton had a couple chunk completion midway through the fourth quarter on Georgia's second-to-last possession, but that was the only time since the first quarter the Tigers failed to dictate the game's tempo.

After trailing by two touchdowns early, Auburn's defense came up with stop after stop to help build a 10-point lead in the second half. The Tigers held Georgia to 113 yards rushing on 28 total carries, including a 2.1 average from Nate Frazier, who was making his return to the lineup.

"Coach (DJ) Durkin, their defensive coordinator, has been one of the best in the conference over all the years he's been in the conference," Smart said before the game. "He's a great defensive football coach. We've got a lot of links, a lot of respect for him. Our guys have to get ready to go play."

Brown finished with 115 yards on the ground for Auburn, along with a 61-yard effort on 13 carries from Jeremiah Cobb. It was the ground and pound approach that worked for Golesh's team against an opponent usually dominant in the trenches.

You can’t really talk about smart glasses without bringing up Meta. HTC, the company behind 2010-era virtual reality headsets and a failed smartphone business, seems quite eager to tackle that comparison directly.

In September, HTC started selling its $499 Vive Eagle smart glasses in the US. The Eagles have lots of the same features as other glasses on the market—cameras for capturing photos and video, speakers in the frames for music playback and calls, an embedded AI agent you can ask questions of and even get recipes from by taking pictures of stuff in your fridge.

But HTC also wants to steer clear of the ongoing debate about privacy in camera-equipped smart glasses. Meta has been dogged by controversy for its smart glasses, with people worried about the company’s interest in enabling face-recognition features, and calling the people who wear them creepy. HTC is aware of that discourse and thinks it is completely possible to make smart glasses that aren’t a privacy nightmare.

“It's not just about protecting the consumer, but it's also about protecting people around the consumer,” Dan McDowell, HTC Vive’s head of enterprise sales, tells WIRED. “People can usher in, I think, what are really tremendous experiences with a new layer of confidence and protection.”

I’ve been wandering around with the glasses for a couple of weeks, and so far they meet my expectations for what smart glasses have become. They protect my eyes from the sun. They snap good photos and videos. You can record and transcribe voice notes. The music playback has decent sound quality. (I’ll always prefer a solid pair of headphones if I’m actually trying to listen to music, but the speakers work just fine.) They come in two styles—one with square Wayfarer-esque lenses and the other more rounded.

The Vive Eagle glasses can get 4.5 hours of battery life on continuous music playback. They can last 36 hours on standby. HTC also sells a companion clip-on battery pack called Power Boost that costs $49. It clips right onto the frame and is noticeable but not as obnoxious as you might think.

Don’t forget the AI assistant, Vive AI, which can utilize OpenAI’s ChatGPT or Google’s Gemini. It doesn’t require a login, so users are “de-identified” in a way that keeps the services from retaining personal information. (That also means, by default, you won’t be able to enjoy many of the personalization features these chatbots offer by gleaning information from your emails and messages.) The glasses come with Vive’s AI Plus, free for the first two years. After that, users must pay a monthly $2.50 subscription fee.

Right by the cameras is a bright indicator light. If you cover the light, it won’t record. If someone around you says stop recording, that will stop the recording. Video footage you capture is encrypted and stored on the glasses—it’s not automatically sent to the phone or cloud. If you want to import photos or videos, you have to do it manually in the app.

Meta has faced scrutiny over the indicator light before, as some users have blocked the LED with stickers or broken into the hardware to turn it off. Meta has responded with software updates that disable the camera if someone tampers with the indicator light, along with other privacy-focused measures.
I ask McDowell how HTC, and really any smart glasses maker, can get past the “trust me, bro”–style privacy promises companies tend to make.

“We're not a social media company,” McDowell says. “There's no benefit to me to have any of your info. We don't train our AI model or any third-party AI models with any of the information that is used on the glasses.”

The real problem may be that with cameras on the frames, smart glasses are hard to distinguish between brands. The Vive Eagles look a lot like Meta glasses, and people worried about those privacy issues may not know that the Eagles are different and not tied to Mark Zuckerberg’s company. I’ve had friends see me wearing them and ask if they’re smart glasses. Yeah, I replied, but not the ones they’re thinking of. That didn’t seem to dispel any of their suspicions.

The hope, at least how HTC frames it, is that more players with better privacy practices will help shift cultural disdain for smart glasses. A bunch of other companies are going cameraless, like Even Realities, Viture, and Halliday. Others are building theirs with privacy shields or focusing on virtual displays instead of capturing the world around you. That said, no one has captured the market quite like Meta.

“We'd like to make sure that our technology adapts to society's expectations, not the other way around,” McDowell says. “I hope that everybody that's making products like these takes steps in the right direction.”

Running a successful parts store requires more than knowing which part fits which vehicle. It takes effective inventory management, dependable delivery service, employees who understand customers’ needs and a manager who can connect everyday decisions to the store’s financial performance.

NAPA is giving independent store owners new resources to develop those capabilities through NAPA Academy, extending training developed for its company-owned stores to independent businesses. The program was introduced during the 2026 NAPA Store Owner and Field Sales Meeting, held Sept. 21-24 in Atlanta. The initial offering focuses on store managers, combining short online courses with a downloadable resource guide designed to help translate training into daily practice.

Introducing the program, Cassie Bell, NAPA’s senior vice president of HR, said the expansion supports the company’s Drive 2030 strategy and its investment in people. Although owners have requested training for several positions, she said store managers were a logical starting point.

“We believe fundamentally that the store manager is critical to obtaining consistent customer service, to building the teams and driving those operational performances inside of our stores,” Bell said.
The program’s development began with a practical question: What do successful employees and stores do differently?

Jesse Parrish, NAPA’s director of learning and development, said the Academy worked with teams across the organization to identify the knowledge, skills and behaviors that define excellence in specific roles. NAPA partnered with industry professionals to turn those findings into training, reference materials and learning pathways.

By observing high-performing managers and market directors in top-performing stores, the team identified the practices and strategies driving their success. Those real-world insights became the foundation for new training programs designed to help others apply proven strategies throughout the organization.

For store operations, the resulting framework has four areas of emphasis: driving financial results, leading and developing teams, enabling operational excellence and delivering exceptional customer service.

Those areas address responsibilities ranging from understanding store performance and building improvement plans to coaching employees, managing inventory, optimizing delivery service and building customer loyalty.
The team documented those practices in how-to guides, training courses and tools intended to help other stores apply them.
The online courses generally take 10 to 20 minutes to complete. Owners can take the courses themselves or assign them to employees, allowing training to address specific development needs.

Although the first offering centers on store management, its usefulness extends to other positions. Parrish pointed to customer service lessons, including effective phone conversations, as examples of content relevant to counter employees.
“It is not just limited to the store manager,” he said. “While the content’s focused on them, there are relevant courses here for others that may be frontline workers working the counter.”

That connection matters because a store’s customer experience depends on both management decisions and individual employee interactions. Training managers to coach their teams complements instruction that helps counter professionals better serve wholesale and retail customers.

The second major resource is a downloadable store manager guide. It outlines the role’s responsibilities, key functions and performance metrics, with linked how-to guidance covering subjects such as budgeting, performance management, customer service and root cause analysis.
Parrish described its purpose in everyday terms: helping employees understand “how do you do the work on a Tuesday morning at nine o’clock?”

The training framework recognizes three proficiency levels: foundation, advanced and mastery. Foundation focuses on performing a job independently and effectively. Advanced emphasizes consistently meeting performance targets and helping others succeed. Mastery involves anticipating opportunities, leading broader improvements and consistently exceeding targets.
That structure provides a development path for employees with different experience levels, from someone entering a management role to an established leader seeking to improve store performance.

Participation is voluntary, Parrish emphasized, with independent owners able to use the resources as they see fit within their businesses. The materials are intended to remain within the NAPA family. NAPA also is exploring how to tailor resources further to independent owners’ needs.

Bell encouraged owners to access the content, develop a plan for using it and return regularly as materials are updated. She also asked them to share feedback about missing resources or opportunities for improvement.

“If you need something more, you need something different, something’s not working, whatever that looks like, please reach back out to us,” Bell said. “We are only as good as the feedback we’re receiving from you.”

Ukraine said on Wednesday that Elon Musk’s SpaceX had restricted “military-grade” Starlink services, hampering Ukrainian drone strike missions and air defenses.
The complaint has drawn renewed attention to the distinction between Starlink, SpaceX’s commercial satellite internet service, and Starshield, a military version developed for the Pentagon.
While Musk has said the two systems are separate, in many cases they share the same underlying satellite technology.

“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government,” Musk said on Wednesday in a post on X, adding that any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military or the president. “Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company.”

Since launching its first Starlink satellites in 2019 aboard reusable SpaceX rockets, the company has built a vast low-Earth-orbit constellation that blankets much of the planet, delivering faster connections than traditional communications satellites, which typically operate much farther from Earth and in far smaller numbers.

Starlink gave Ukraine a critical communications advantage early in the war, reshaping how militaries operate on the battlefield. But Musk has restricted Starlink for certain military uses while highlighting Starshield, a more secure network developed for government and military missions.
Starshield is a SpaceX business unit that develops military and intelligence satellite systems for the Pentagon.

While its missions are separate from Starlink’s commercial broadband service, the distinction is not always clear-cut: Starshield’s secure communications services use enhanced encryption and dedicated terminals, but rely on the vast Starlink constellation as their backbone.

Starshield leverages the technology, engineering and operational experiences of Starlink, according to SpaceX. In addition to secure communications, the company says the militarized version can also provide users with Earth observation and the ability to integrate sensors or other payloads.

The Pentagon, Starshield’s largest customer, has spent billions of dollars on both Starlink and Starshield services. It has also bought dedicated Starshield satellites, including communications spacecraft for missile-warning missions and a spy constellation for the National Reconnaissance Office, Reuters reported in 2024.

Questions over the relationship between Starlink and Starshield have persisted since Russia threatened Western satellites supporting Ukraine in 2022. SpaceX unveiled Starshield later that year, but the secrecy surrounding national security space programs has left the precise boundaries between the two systems opaque.

Those distinctions became a point of contention earlier this year when the Pentagon clashed with SpaceX over higher prices for satellite services used by military drones during the Iran conflict, Reuters reported.
SpaceX argued that some customers paying roughly $5,000 per terminal for Starlink should instead have been using a Starshield service costing about $25,000 per terminal.

Britain has also adopted Starshield. Under that arrangement, the service uses the same satellite constellation, ground stations and terrestrial infrastructure as Starlink, but operates through dedicated terminals and separate network gateways, Britain’s defense ministry has told Reuters.

Other U.S. partners are evaluating the system as well. New Zealand is doing a trial of Starshield to assess its usefulness for military operations, the New Zealand Defence Force previously told Reuters.
